opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think SWE-bench was a really useful benchmark for a while, but it captures a pretty narrow slice of what software engineering actually is. Each task is basically: here's a GitHub issue in a well-known Python repo, here's the codebase, go write a patch that makes some hidden unit tests pass. That's real work, but it's very well-scoped work. Someone has already done the hard part of figuring out what the problem is, isolating it, and writing it up clearly. And the tasks are mostly small, in the range of something a competent engineer might knock out in an hour or so.

Real software engineering is much messier. A huge amount of the job is ambiguity resolution: talking to people, figuring out what you're actually supposed to build, understanding an enormous codebase with lots of implicit context that isn't written down anywhere, and making judgment calls about architecture that won't pay off or blow up until months later. SWE-bench doesn't test any of that. It also doesn't test long-horizon work, where you're chaining together dozens or hundreds of steps, recovering from your own mistakes, and keeping a coherent plan over days rather than minutes.

There's also the measurement issue. Passing unit tests is a proxy for "did you solve the problem well." You can pass the tests with a patch that a senior engineer would never merge because it's hacky, or it breaks something the tests don't cover. And once a benchmark becomes the thing everyone optimizes for, it saturates, and you start learning more about how well people have fit the benchmark than about underlying capability.

So the way I'd frame it is that SWE-bench tells you whether the model can do the atomic unit of a software task. What actually matters for automating software engineering is whether you can string those atomic units together reliably over long time horizons, with minimal supervision, in messy real-world environments. That's the frontier now, and I think the more interesting metrics look like: how long a task, measured in human hours, can the model complete autonomously at some reliability threshold? And how is that number growing? That trend line tells you a lot more about where we're headed than any single benchmark score.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing to understand about SWE-bench is that it was a really good benchmark for its time, and it still tells you something, but it's measuring a pretty narrow slice of what software engineering actually is. It's a set of GitHub issues from a handful of mostly Python open-source repos, and the task is: here's the issue, here's the repo, make the hidden tests pass. That's a real task, people do that every day, but it's maybe the most legible, most self-contained version of the job.

The first limitation is just the time horizon. These are tasks that a good engineer would do in, you know, fifteen minutes to a couple of hours. Nothing in there is "we need to migrate this service to a new database over the next three weeks" or "figure out why latency regressed across these four systems." And the thing we actually care about for automation is whether the model can take on long-horizon work, where it has to hold a plan, make intermediate decisions, recover from being wrong, and keep going without someone correcting it every ten minutes. SWE-bench doesn't really stress that. You can be very good at SWE-bench and still fall over on anything that takes a day.

The second thing is the environment is kind of pre-chewed for you. The problem is already specified. Someone has written the issue, someone has written the tests, you know what "done" looks like. A huge amount of real software engineering is figuring out what the problem even is: talking to the person who filed the bug, realizing the ticket is wrong, deciding what not to do, pushing back on scope. None of that shows up. And relatedly, the verification is unusually clean. Most real work doesn't come with a hidden test suite that tells you unambiguously whether you got it right. You have to construct your own notion of correctness, and that's a skill the benchmark gives you for free.

Third, and this is the one people underweight, is contamination and overfitting in a soft sense. Not that the exact solutions are in the training data necessarily, though some of them might be, but these are popular repos, the style of problem is very well represented, and once a benchmark becomes the thing everyone optimizes against, you start seeing improvements that are real on the benchmark and don't generalize as much as the number suggests. The Verified subset helped with the noise, but it doesn't fix the fact that the distribution is narrow.

So the way I'd put it is: SWE-bench going from, say, forty to eighty percent is genuinely meaningful, it tracks something, and I don't want to be dismissive of it. But it's a floor, not a ceiling, on what you need to know. The questions I'd actually want answered about software automation are more like: how long can the agent work unsupervised before its errors compound? Can it operate in a messy, large, proprietary codebase that it's never seen? Can it do the ambiguous, cross-cutting work rather than the well-posed patch? Those are the things that determine whether you've automated a task or automated a job, and we need benchmarks that are much closer to the shape of real work to get at them.

astra-6.text:
SWE-bench mostly asks, “Given an existing codebase and a well-specified issue, can you produce a patch that passes the tests?” That’s a useful capability to measure, but it’s a much narrower task than being a software engineer.

A lot of the work is figuring out what to build, understanding requirements that nobody has written down properly, and making decisions whose consequences show up months later. You can solve an individual issue while making the overall system harder to maintain. Passing the tests doesn’t necessarily tell you whether you made a good engineering decision.

There’s also a gap between solving a substantial fraction of isolated tasks and reliably owning a project. If a human has to work out which tasks to delegate, provide all the context, and catch the failures, that human can still be the bottleneck. So I’d want to know how long the model can work independently, and how much supervision it needs to deliver something useful. SWE-bench gives you some evidence about that, but it doesn’t directly measure it.

sol-6.1.text:
SWE-bench measures something real, but it’s a fairly narrow slice of software engineering. You’re given an existing repository and a specific issue, and success is roughly: can you produce a patch that passes the tests? That’s much easier to specify and evaluate than “build something people want.”

A lot of the work is figuring out what the software should do, understanding constraints that nobody wrote down, making architectural decisions, and then operating and maintaining the thing. You can get very good at fixing well-defined bugs without being able to take responsibility for that whole process.

There’s also a time-horizon issue. Solving a task that takes a human an hour doesn’t tell you whether the model can work coherently for a week, notice that an earlier assumption was wrong, and recover without somebody steering it. So I’d take improvements on SWE-bench seriously as evidence of coding capability. I’d be much more cautious about translating the score directly into a percentage of software engineering jobs automated.
